source_text: Iam igitur ad eum convertamur. Dederas mihi peccatum opus esse voluntatis; potui statim dicere consequenter: Voluntas autem, quae peccet, in parvulis nulla est; peccatum igitur in parvulis non est. Verum ut pluribus premereris testibus, interrogavi sensim, per quid hoc peccatum inveniretur in parvulo; ne forte per voluntatem? Post quod, te connivente, suscepi nullam in eo fuisse conscientiam voluntatis; adiunxi, ne per primam culpam membrorum lineamenta traxisset. Sed haec a Deo informari, et per hoc bona esse concesseras. Petivi tertium, utrum per ingressum animae, reatum advectum putares. Sed hanc esse novam, ne quidquam seminibus debere constabat. Intuli deinceps, ne (quia nihil tibi de his remanserat arguendum) nuptias, id est commixtionem corporum, diaboli opus vocares? Sed has pertinere ad parentum operam, te quoque annuente, monstravi. Illis igitur omnibus quae supra diximus absolutis, coniuges qui fuerant causa peccati, tradux tua diabolo mancipabat. Post quae omnia, quod tibi propinquabat impegi, ut dicerem credere te diabolum auctorem corporum, cui commixtionis operam, sine qua origo corporum esse non poterat, deputasses. Et haec quidem disputatio, quo morbo oppressus esses, ostendit; illa autem secunda, et te miserabilem cum eiusmodi sensibus, et Catholicos etiam timoris tui suffragio invictos probavit. Te enim dante, a Deo fieri homines, et esse coniuges innocentes, ac parvulos per se nihil operari; his tribus sumptis, irrefutabiliter illatum est, cum non peccat ille qui nascitur, non peccat ille qui genuit, non peccat iste qui condidit, nullam remansisse rimam, per quam peccatum doceatur ingressum. Tibi ergo si displicet quod collectum est; abnue quod dedisti, et dic aut illum peccasse qui genuit, aut illum qui condidit, aut istum qui natus est; ex quibus unum insanum est, aliud Manichaeum, tertium supra Manichaeos; insanum, si dixeris delinquere parvulos; Manichaeum, si accusaveris coniuges, supra Manichaeos, si peccati Deum aestimaris auctorem. Quod si haec omnia tam aliena sunt a vero, ut adhuc ea metuas libere confiteri; qua impudentia, homo omnium amentissime, hoc quod a nobis illatum est, persistis negare?
pass_a_gloss: Now therefore let us turn to him. You had given me that sin is a work of will; I could at once say consequently: But a will which sins is none in little children; sin therefore is not in little children. But that you might be pressed by more witnesses, I asked gradually through what this sin would be found in a little child; lest perhaps through will? After which, with you winking, I took up that there had been in him no consciousness of will; I added, lest through the first fault he had drawn the lineaments of the members. But you had granted that these are formed by God, and through this are good. I sought a third, whether through the entrance of the soul you thought a reatus brought in. But it stood that this soul is new, lest it owe anything to seeds. I brought in next, lest (because nothing of these had remained for you to be accused) you should call marriages, that is the mingling of bodies, a work of the devil? But I showed, with you also nodding, that these belong to the parents' work. Those things therefore which we said above having been acquitted, the spouses who had been the cause of sin your tradux was making over to the devil. After all which I struck what was drawing near to you, so that I might say that you believe the devil to be the author of bodies, to whom you had assigned the work of mingling, without which an origin of bodies could not be. And this disputation, indeed, showed by what disease you had been oppressed; but that second proved both you pitiable with senses of this kind, and catholics unconquered even by the vote of your fear. For with you giving that human beings are made by God, and that spouses are innocent, and that little children through themselves work nothing; these three premises having been taken, it was irrefutably inferred that, since he who is born does not sin, he who begot does not sin, this one who founded does not sin, no crack has remained through which sin may be taught to have entered. If therefore what has been collected displeases you; refuse what you have given, and say either that he sinned who begot, or he who founded, or this one who has been born; of which one is insane, another Manichaean, the third above the Manichaeans; insane, if you shall have said that little children offend; Manichaean, if you shall have accused spouses, above the Manichaeans, if you shall have estimated God the author of sin. Which if all these things are so alien from the true that you still fear to confess them freely; with what shamelessness, most mindless of all men, do you persist in denying this which has been inferred by us?

pass_b_english: Let us now turn to him. You had granted me that sin is an act of the will. I could immediately have said, as a consequence: ‘But infants have no will that sins; therefore infants have no sin.’ Yet to press you with more witnesses I asked, step by step, through what this sin could be found in an infant. Could it perhaps be through the will? Then, with your acquiescence, I adopted the premise that the infant had had no consciousness of willing. I added the question whether the infant had acquired the outlines of its limbs through the first fault. But you had conceded that God shapes them and that they are therefore good. Third, I asked whether you thought guilt was brought in through the soul’s arrival. Yet it was established that this soul was new and owed nothing to the seed. Next I asked whether, since nothing in these things remained for you to accuse, you called marriage—that is, the union of bodies—the devil’s work. But, again with your agreement, I showed that this belongs to the parents’ activity. Once everything mentioned above had been acquitted, your doctrine of transmission enslaved to the devil the married people who had caused the sin. After all this I drove home the consequence approaching you: you believe the devil is the creator of bodies, since you assigned to him the work of sexual union without which bodies could not originate. This argument showed the disease oppressing you. The second showed both how pitiable you are with such views and how invincible the catholics remain, supported even by your fear. You conceded that God makes human beings, that married people are innocent, and that infants perform no acts on their own. From these three premises it was irrefutably inferred that, when the one born does not sin, the one who fathered the child does not sin, and the one who created the child does not sin, no crack remains through which sin can be shown to have entered. If you dislike the conclusion, then deny your concession. Say that either the one who fathered the child sinned, or the one who created the child, or the child who was born. Of these alternatives, one is insane, another Manichaean, and the third goes beyond the Manichaeans: insane if you say infants commit offenses; Manichaean if you accuse married people; beyond the Manichaeans if you consider God the author of sin. But if all these things are so far from the truth that you still fear to confess them openly, with what shamelessness, most senseless of men, do you persist in denying the conclusion we have drawn?

choices.why: Bodily seed of generation; Julian denies it carries a will's sin.
Parents insofar as parents are not guilty; keep the forensic 'in quantum parentes sunt'.
